items.stem: Which question could you answer with a measurement you can actually take this week?

options.label: How many students use the library between 3 and 4 pm?
Is the library a good place?
Do students value learning?

items.hint_text: Look for the question you can count or time.
items.feedback_correct: Yes. Counting students in a set hour is a measurement you can repeat and compare.
items.feedback_wrong: Counting students in a set hour is a measurement you can repeat and compare. Good or value are opinions with no number attached.

items.stem: Which of these questions is too big to investigate with the time you have?

options.label: Why do people like the city?
How many people cross this street in ten minutes?
How long is the wait at this bus stop at 8 am?

items.hint_text: If you cannot picture the measurement, the question is too big.
items.feedback_correct: Right. Why people like the city has no clear measurement and would need a large study.
items.feedback_wrong: Why people like the city has no clear measurement and would need a large study. Counting crossings or timing a wait are small, answerable measurements.

items.stem: Which questions are testable with a small measurement? Select all that apply.

options.label: How many people use this bench in an hour?
What is the average wait at the bus stop?
Is this neighborhood happy?
How many students bring lunch from home?

items.hint_text: Testable questions describe something you can count or time.
items.feedback_correct: Yes. Counting users, averaging a wait, and counting lunches are all measurable.
items.feedback_wrong: Testable questions describe something you can count or time. Asking if a neighborhood is happy is an opinion with no number you can collect.

items.stem: The module says a small sample you actually took is better than what?

options.label: A big number you guessed
A careful count you did
A short honest measurement

items.hint_text: The alternative is not measured at all.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. A real small sample beats an invented big number.
items.feedback_wrong: The point is that real, small measurements beat invented big ones. A careful count or an honest measurement is exactly the good option, not the alternative.

items.stem: Which actions keep a small sample honest? Select all that apply.

options.label: Write down the number you actually counted
Record when and where you measured
Round up to a nicer number
Skip measurements you dislike

items.hint_text: Honest data is recorded as it was, with time and place.
items.feedback_correct: Right. Recording the true count and the time and place keeps the sample honest.
items.feedback_wrong: An honest sample records what you truly measured, with the time and place. Changing numbers you dislike or rounding up makes the data untrustworthy.

items.stem: What makes a question answerable in a small investigation?

options.label: You can picture the measurement you would take
It sounds impressive and broad
It has no clear end

items.hint_text: Think about whether you can see the measurement.
items.feedback_correct: Yes. If you can picture the measurement, the question is answerable.
items.feedback_wrong: A question is answerable when you can picture exactly what you would measure. Broad or endless questions cannot be finished with the time you have.

items.stem: Which question is testable with a simple count?

options.label: How many bikes are parked here at noon?
Are people friendly here?
Should the city add more parks?

items.hint_text: One option can be counted directly.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. Counting parked bikes is a measurement you can repeat.
items.feedback_wrong: Counting bikes is a measurement you can repeat. Friendly and should questions are opinions, not something you can count.

items.stem: Which questions could you answer with a small measurement this week? Select all that apply.

options.label: How many cars pass this corner in ten minutes?
How long does the crossing light stay green?
Is this the best street in town?
How many flyers are left on the shelf?

items.hint_text: A testable question points at something you can count or time.
items.feedback_correct: Right. Counting cars, timing the light, and counting flyers are all measurable.
items.feedback_wrong: A testable question points at something you can count or time. Asking if this is the best street is an opinion with no measurement behind it.

items.stem: You can only observe for ten minutes. What should you do?

options.label: Take the small sample you can and note it
Guess the number for the rest of the day
Wait for a bigger budget

items.hint_text: A small real sample still counts.
items.feedback_correct: Yes. A small sample you actually took is honest and useful.
items.feedback_wrong: A small sample you actually took is honest and useful. Guessing or waiting leaves you with no real data at all.

items.stem: Why is a small honest sample more useful than a large guessed number?

options.label: You can trust and check what you measured
It is always more accurate than a big sample
It removes the need to record anything

items.hint_text: The value is that the sample is real.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. The sample is real and checkable, so you can trust it.
items.feedback_wrong: The value is that the sample is real and checkable, not that it beats every larger study. You still need to record what you measured.
